summary: This memo describes an overall strategy for deploying a Directory Service on the Internet, based on the OSI X.500 Directory Service. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a giant online phone book for the whole Internet. This paper is a plan for building it, one step at a time.

questions: how to build a global directory
subtitle: A roadmap for building a global Internet directory based on the X.500 standard.

tldr.problem: The Internet lacked a unified directory service for looking up user information, locating resources, and managing infrastructure. DNS was insufficient for these purposes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1430 proposes deploying X.500, an OSI directory standard, as the basis for an Internet Directory Service, with a hierarchical information framework managed nationally and by organizations.
tldr.outcome: This was an informational document outlining strategy; actual deployment happened through systems like LDAP and DNS extensions rather than pure X.500, but it established key architectural concepts still used today.

today: RFC 1430 was an informational document outlining strategy, not a specification. While pure X.500 deployment on the Internet never happened at the scale envisioned, the architectural concepts influenced actual directory deployments. LDAP, standardized later, became the lightweight protocol for directory access. DNS continued to serve domain name lookup, while LDAP directories became common within organizations.

sections.title: The Need for a Global Directory
sections.content:
The early Internet had no unified way to find users, look up organizational information, or discover resources. RFC 1430 recognizes several immediate needs: a white pages service to find people, support for X.509 certificates needed for secure mail, and resource location across the Internet.

The document proposes building an Internet-wide directory service based on X.500, an OSI standard already in use in Europe and early pilots. Rather than centralizing everything, it envisions a distributed directory where each organization or nation manages its own part of the tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine if you couldn't look up anyone's email or find servers. This RFC says we need a big shared address book, with each country keeping their own list and organizations managing their entries.

sections.title: The X.500 Information Framework
sections.content:
X.500 provides a hierarchical structure called the Directory Information Tree (DIT). Each entry represents an object (a person, organization, or service) with attributes (name, email, organization) and a distinguished name that uniquely identifies it globally. The model allows multiple inheritance through object classes, making it flexible for different types of data.

The RFC describes three layers: the technical model (how data is stored and typed), extensions needed for Internet use (support for management information and non-hierarchical searching), and the operational model where large organizations run their own Directory System Agents (DSAs) and smaller ones rent space from regional providers.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like an organizational chart: each person is a box with their details, grouped under their organization, which sits under their country. Everything has a unique address you can look up.

sections.title: How Names Are Assigned
sections.content:
The document proposes a country-based naming structure where each nation manages its part of the directory tree. Within each country, registration authorities (similar to domain registrars) would assign names to organizations, which then manage names for people and services within them.

This balances flexibility with consistency: each country can use its own naming conventions below the country level, but the top-level structure remains coordinated. The RFC notes that in North America, the North American Directory Forum was exploring this, while the Internet Society might serve as the naming authority globally.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory tree would start with countries at the top (US, UK, France), then organizations within each country, then people within organizations. Each level assigns names to the level below.

sections.title: Infrastructure and Phased Rollout
sections.content:
The deployment plan calls for several layers of infrastructure. Short-term requirements include establishing a root DSA (managed by the Paradise project at the time), coordinating name assignment across regions, and managing replication of directory data for performance. A lightweight protocol over TCP/IP (which became LDAP) was identified as essential for reaching low-powered workstations.

Medium-term goals include enhanced performance and expanded schema to support mail handling, NIC data, and resource location. Long-term work involves evolving X.500 as standards mature, integrating existing relational databases into the directory, and improving performance for resource location.
sections.plainLanguage: First, set up the main office (root directory). Then connect regional offices, each managing their area. Gradually add more services and make it faster.

sections.title: Technical Challenges to Solve
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several gaps between X.500 as standardized and what the Internet needs. The standard lacked sufficient detail on replication and caching, which are critical for performance across a global network. The document proposed interim solutions using approaches like relay DSAs and distributed operations.

Other challenges included handling different network stacks (TCP/IP, OSI, X.25), representing network addresses across incompatible lower layers, and providing a user-friendly string representation of directory names instead of the formal distinguished name syntax. The RFC also notes the need for mechanisms to register new attributes and object classes as requirements evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: The challenge was making X.500 work over the Internet's TCP/IP, handling data stored far apart, representing names in ways humans can read, and keeping everything coordinated as people add new types of information.

sections.title: Security and Data Management
sections.content:
The directory could become a key component of Internet security by storing X.509 certificates and authentication information. The RFC discusses several security services: peer authentication at bind time, per-operation authentication using digital signatures, and access control to prevent both individual entry tampering and unauthorized searching.

The RFC emphasizes that distributed data management is a feature, not a bug: each organization maintains its own entries, improving accuracy. However, it requires data quality guidelines and legal consideration of privacy laws, which differ by country. The document recommends drafting a user bill of rights defining appropriate use of the directory.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory needs to protect people's privacy and prevent misuse. Each country follows its own privacy laws. Organizations keep their own data honest, and the directory can store security certificates people need for encrypted mail.
